statement_record.book: In a locally small C, h : y -> z induces a natural transformation h_* : C(-,y) => C(-,z) of contravariant represented functors by postcomposition, and f : w -> x induces f^* : C(x,-) => C(w,-) of covariant represented functors by precomposition; in both cases the naturality square C(x,y) -> C(x,z), C(w,y) -> C(w,z) commutes because the two routes send g : x -> y to the same composite hgf, i.e. by associativity.
statement_record.intree: Curried_Hom C : C^op ⟶ [C, Sets] has, on f : x ~{C^op}~> y, the transformation with components `fun g => g ∘ op f` (the precomposition clause, with functoriality in f); Yoneda_Embedding C : ∀ A B, Presheaves [Hom ─,A] [Hom ─,B] ≊ A ~> B identifies the postcomposition transformations C(−,A) ⟹ C(−,B) with the morphisms A ~> B; and Hom C : C^op ∏ C ⟶ Sets is the two-variable hom-bifunctor whose fmap is `fun g => snd f ∘ g ∘ fst f`, its functor law discharged by `now rewrite !comp_assoc` — literally the book's 'commutativity is associativity of composition'.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same (setoid rephrasing: hom-sets are hom-setoids and the naturality square is stated up to ≈). If anything intree-stronger for the postcomposition clause: Yoneda_Embedding gives a bijection with A ~> B, not merely that postcomposition is natural. Riehl's local-smallness hypothesis is not needed here: the library's hom-setoids are objects of Sets by construction.

statement_record.book: In Set the four isomorphisms A x (B + C) ≅ (A x B) + (A x C), A^(B+C) ≅ A^B x A^C, (A x B)^C ≅ A^C x B^C, (A^B)^C ≅ A^(B x C) are NATURAL — the first a natural isomorphism of functors Set x Set x Set -> Set, the exponential ones contravariant in the exponent variable and arising from the two-sided represented bifunctor Set^op x Set -> Set. Restricting along the groupoid Fin_iso of finite sets and bijections and applying the cardinality functor |-| : Fin_iso -> N (into the discrete category of naturals) DECATEGORIFIES them into a x (b+c) = ab + ac, a^(b+c) = a^b a^c, (ab)^c = a^c b^c, (a^b)^c = a^(bc); conversely Fin_iso categorifies N.
statement_record.intree: All four isomorphisms are proved as object-indexed families in an arbitrary Cartesian + Cocartesian + Closed category (`Section BiCCC`, `Context {C : Category}` with `@Cartesian C`, `@Cocartesian C`, `@Closed C _`), hence hold in Coq (Coq_Cartesian/Coq_Closed/Coq_Cocartesian/Coq_Initial, Instance/Coq.v:141,167,187,199) and in Sets (Instance/Sets/Cartesian.v, Instance/Sets/Cocartesian.v, Instance/Sets/Cartesian/Closed.v). Theory/Algebra.v:68-88 is a `Goal ... auto. Qed.` index restating exactly these as the rig laws, with the file header calling the section 'categorified high-school algebra'.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker on two counts: (1) each isomorphism is an object-indexed FAMILY of isomorphisms, not a natural isomorphism — no naturality square in x, y, z (nor the contravariance in the exponent) is stated or proved for prod_coprod_r, exp_coprod, exp_prod_r or exp_prod_l anywhere in the tree; (2) the decategorification half is entirely absent.

evidence.intree_statement: Theorem Functor_Setoid_Nat_Iso `(F : C ⟶ D) (G : C ⟶ D) : F ≅[Fun] G  ↔  F ≈ G.   (* where `F ≈ G` is Functor_Setoid, Theory/Functor.v:148: `{ iso : ∀ x : C, F x ≅ G x & ∀ (x y : C) (f : x ~> y), fmap[F] f ≈ from (iso y) ∘ fmap[G] f ∘ to (iso x) }` — a componentwise-invertible natural family *)
Definition equiv_iso {C D : Category} {f g : C ⟶ D} : f ≈ g → f ≅[Fun] g := snd (Functor_Setoid_Nat_Iso _ _).

statement_record.book: If alpha : F => G is a natural isomorphism (a natural transformation each of whose components is an isomorphism), then the inverses of its components are themselves the components of a natural transformation alpha^{-1} : G => F, which is inverse to alpha.
statement_record.intree: `Functor_Setoid_Nat_Iso : F ≅[Fun] G ↔ F ≈ G`, whose right-to-left direction (packaged standalone as `equiv_iso : f ≈ g → f ≅[Fun] g`) takes a family of componentwise isomorphisms `∀ x, F x ≅ G x` satisfying the naturality condition and produces an isomorphism in the functor category [C, D] — i.e. it constructs the inverse natural transformation from the componentwise inverses and discharges its naturality square (the second `+ transform; simpl; intros. * apply x. * abstract (rewrite e; simpl; rewrite <- !comp_assoc; rewrite iso_to_from; cat)` block at Instance/Fun.v:284-293).
statement_record.strength_comparison: same. The in-tree hypothesis `F ≈ G` is the conjugated form `fmap[F] f ≈ from (iso y) ∘ fmap[G] f ∘ to (iso x)` of Riehl's naturality square, equivalent to it because each component is invertible; the conclusion `F ≅[Fun] G` is an isomorphism in [C, D], i.e. exactly a natural transformation back with both composites the identity. The library also gets the converse direction (invertible in [C, D] ⟹ componentwise invertible) in the same iff, which the exercise does not ask for.

statement_record.intree: Yoneda_Embedding C : ∀ A B : C, Presheaves [Hom ─,A] [Hom ─,B] ≊ A ~> B  (the postcomposition assignment A ~> B → Nat(C(−,A), C(−,B)) is an isomorphism of setoids, hence injective); Covariant_Yoneda_Embedding C : ∀ A B : C, Copresheaves [Hom B,─] [Hom A,─] ≊ A ~> B  (the precomposition assignment is likewise an isomorphism). The bare injectivity of the precomposition clause is additionally isolated as `#[export] Instance Yoneda_Faithful (C : Category) : Faithful (Curried_Hom C)` (Functor/Hom.v:85), proved by evaluating the transformation at the identity — exactly the book's argument.

Setoid rephrasing: 'distinct' means ≉ in the hom-setoid, and injectivity is up to ≈ on both sides.

evidence.intree_statement: Class Dinatural := { ditransform {x} : F (x, x) ~> G (x, x); dinaturality {x y} (f : x ~{C}~> y) : fmap[G] (op f ⋆⋆⋆ id) ∘ @ditransform y ∘ fmap[F] (id ⋆⋆⋆ f) ≈ fmap[G] (id ⋆⋆⋆ f) ∘ @ditransform x ∘ fmap[F] (op f ⋆⋆⋆ id) }   (* Context {F G : C^op ∏ C ⟶ D}; `f ⋆⋆⋆ g` = prod_split, packaging a C^op-component and a C-component *)
Class Wedge `(F : C^op ∏ C ⟶ D) := { wedge_obj : D; wedge_map {x : C} : wedge_obj ~{D}~> F (x, x); ump_wedges {x y : C} (f : x ~{C}~> y) : bimap[F] id f ∘ wedge_map ≈ bimap[F] (op f) id ∘ wedge_map }

statement_record.book: For F, G : C^op x C -> D, a family alpha_c : F(c,c) -> G(c,c) indexed by objects c defines a DINATURAL transformation alpha : F => G if for every f : c -> c' the hexagon commutes: G(id,f) . alpha_c . F(f,id) = G(f,id) . alpha_{c'} . F(id,f) as maps F(c',c) -> G(c,c'). Then specialize this condition to the case where F and G arise by restricting a covariant H : C -> D and a contravariant K : C^op -> D along the projections pi_2 and pi_1.
statement_record.intree: `Class Dinatural` over `Context {F G : C^op ∏ C ⟶ D}` with the diagonal component `ditransform {x} : F (x, x) ~> G (x, x)` and the hexagon `dinaturality`, stated in the library's variance-explicit `⋆⋆⋆` notation with both sides typed F (y,x) ~> G (x,y). The file header spells the hexagon out as 'G f x ∘ α_x ∘ F f x ≈ G x f ∘ α_y ∘ F x f'.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same for the definitional content — same variance convention (contravariant first argument), same diagonal components, same six-edge condition, transcribed up to ≈. Two riders, neither of which is a weakening of the stated hexagon: (a) the library deliberately provides no identity/composition for Dinatural (header: 'dinatural transformations do NOT compose in general'), which the exercise does not need; (b) the exercise's SECOND clause — specializing the hexagon to F = H ◯ pi_2 and G = K ◯ pi_1 for a covariant H and contravariant K — is not separately recorded.
